# The Exercises and Professional Competencies {#sec-appendix-competencies}

This appendix maps the book's exercises, comprehensive cases, and capstone cases to the competency areas of four frameworks that accounting programs use to plan courses and to document what their students learn. It is written for instructors who align a course with the CPA Evolution model curriculum, with the management accounting competencies of the Institute of Management Accountants (IMA), with the International Education Standards of the International Federation of Accountants (IFAC), or with the accounting accreditation standards of AACSB International. An entry means that the item practices the competency as one of its main tasks, not that it covers everything the framework expects. Each item appears in at most three rows of each framework's table, the ones its requirements exercise most directly, and a row can group related competencies or topics.

The tables use short labels. A number such as 6.5 is Exercise 6.5, B.1 is an exercise of [the appendix on publishing, securing, and sharing reports](#sec-appendix-publishing), and C.1 one of [the appendix on Power BI in the browser](#sec-appendix-browser). Part II R5 is Requirement 5 of the comprehensive case that closes Part II, and Ch. 19 R4 is Requirement 4 of the capstone case in Chapter 19. The tables cover the book's applied work, every exercise and every numbered requirement of the comprehensive and capstone cases, and each of them appears at least once in each table. The guided tutorials and the multiple-choice questions are not mapped.


## The Frameworks

The CPA Evolution model curriculum of the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA) and the National Association of State Boards of Accountancy (NASBA), in its update of November 2021, is a sample curriculum developed to help faculty prepare their students for the CPA profession (AICPA & NASBA, 2021). It shows what a program can teach and is not a blueprint of the CPA Exam. Its core covers accounting and data analytics, audit and accounting information systems, and tax, and three disciplines build on it. @tbl-d-01 uses the curriculum's own structure: Core S1 is the core section on accounting and data analytics, Core S2 the core section on audit and accounting information systems, BAR the business analysis and reporting discipline, and ISC the information systems and controls discipline, each followed by the module (M) and, where it matters, the topic (T).

IMA's expanded management accounting competency framework organizes the competencies of management accountants into ten domains, each with embedded competencies described at three proficiency tiers: foundational, proficient, and expert (IMA, 2025). @tbl-d-02 lists the domains and competencies that the book practices. It leaves the tier to the instructor, because the same item can be assigned at different depths, and the tier a student reaches shows in the student's work, not in the item.

IFAC's International Education Standards set out the competence that aspiring professional accountants develop by the end of their initial professional development. The versions issued in 2025 are effective from July 1, 2026. IES 2 sets out the areas of technical competence, IES 3 the professional skills, and IES 4 the professional values, ethics, and attitudes (IFAC, 2025a, 2025b, 2025c). @tbl-d-03 uses the standards' area letters, such as IES 2 (i) for information and communications technologies, adds the number of a learning outcome where a row rests on one, as in IES 2 (i)(iv), and paraphrases the outcomes.

AACSB International's standards for accounting accreditation include Standard A5, Digital Agility. It expects the curriculum to integrate the technologies of accounting practice, students to judge whether a technology fits a task and to interpret and communicate its results, and students to learn new technologies as the profession changes (AACSB International, 2026). @tbl-d-04 maps the items to the standard's three parts, with Part 5.1 divided by the tool each item uses. In the 5.2 row, Exercises 12.6, 13.4, 15.2, and 15.5 ask students to judge whether a method or a tool fits a task, and 6.5, 7.6, 13.6, and C.3 to read a tool's output or limits with skepticism. The exercises of Chapters 1 and 3 practice a foundational step, deciding which records a question needs, and the case and capstone requirements in the row mostly interpret and communicate results.


## Using the Map

The tables work in two directions. To choose assignments, start from a competency that the course must cover and pick from the items in its row. To document a course, start from the items the course assigns and collect the rows in which they appear.

An entry marks an opportunity to practice a competency, not evidence that a student has attained it or reached a given IMA tier. To use an item as evidence, record the outcome it assesses, the work each student submits, the rubric and its threshold, and how individual performance is checked. The solutions on the [Downloads](#sec-downloads) page give reference results for grading, and a submission that matches them is not by itself evidence of competence.

AACSB's Table A5, which lists the technologies of each course, leaves out ordinary productivity software such as Microsoft Office (AACSB International, 2026). For the Excel work, name the functionality each assignment uses, such as Power Query, PivotTables, the Analysis ToolPak, or Solver, rather than relabeling ordinary worksheet work, and confirm with the program's accreditation lead how the table should treat it. The SQL and Power BI work fits the table as it is.

The items in the 5.3 row carry an analysis that students already know into another tool or setting, such as Chapter 8's tests into SQL or a Power BI model into the browser. They become evidence for 5.3, which asks students to learn new technologies independently, only when the instructor adds a task in which students learn a feature the book does not teach from its documentation, apply it to the problem, and check the result against a control total.

The tables use the November 2021 update of the CPA Evolution model curriculum, IMA's 2025 framework, the IFAC standards effective from July 1, 2026, and AACSB's 2026 accounting standards. The frameworks change more often than the exercises do, so check which version applies to a program, and which edition of the standards governs its accreditation review, before relying on a code from these tables.
